name: what with Circumstantial Adjunct
pattern: adjunct[what with + NP, non-finite or verbless predication, or coordination]

entry.name: what with Circumstantial Adjunct
entry.pattern: adjunct[what with + NP, non-finite or verbless predication, or coordination]

1.definition: Presents one or more circumstances as explaining the main situation.
1.details: What with the trains being late describes a reason for the delay. A plain with phrase can also depict an accompanying circumstance with no explanatory force, as in She waited with her arms folded. Adding what invites a reason reading. A simple NP such as the weather can fill the same slot.

examples.form: [What with the trains being late and the roads blocked], we stayed put.
[What with the weather], we never left the house.
examples.note: Constructed example with a simple NP.

relatedConstructions.notes: Both can express circumstances with their own predication.
The form includes fixed with and can contain an NP.

grounds.note: Tests addition of what in the depictive use.
Records the reason adjunct and the coordinated complement.

projection.target: Adding what to the relevant with frame imposes an explanatory interpretation. Its complement can also be a simple circumstance-denoting NP.
projection.evidence: FrameNet tests explanatory versus depictive interpretations. CGEL records what with as an idiom introducing a reason adjunct.

curious.title: What with, giving reasons
curious.summary: What with and one or more circumstances offers them as the reason for what happened.
curious.body: What with the trains being late and the roads blocked, we stayed put. The part before the comma lists the circumstances, and they explain why we stayed. A simple noun phrase can fill the same slot: What with the weather, we never left the house. A plain with phrase can show an accompanying circumstance with no explanation, as in She waited with her arms folded. Adding what invites a reason reading. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.

examples.text: [What with the trains being late and the roads blocked], we stayed put.
[What with the weather], we never left the house.
She waited with her arms folded.

curious.try: Explain why you were late using What with and two reasons. Does it sound like an excuse?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes, what with as a way to present circumstances as the reason for a situation.
teacher.explain: The pattern is an adjunct beginning with what with, followed by a noun phrase, a non-finite or verbless predication, or a coordination. It presents one or more circumstances as explaining the main situation. A plain with phrase can depict an accompanying circumstance with no explanatory force, as in She waited with her arms folded. Adding what invites a reason reading. A simple noun phrase such as the weather can fill the same slot. This dictionary marks its analysis provisional.
teacher.terms: This dictionary treats what with as an idiom introducing a reason adjunct, and relates it to absolute supplements, which can also express circumstances with their own predication.

examples.text: [What with the trains being late and the roads blocked], we stayed put.
[What with the weather], we never left the house.

contrasts.text: What with the weather, we never left the house.
She waited with her arms folded.

watch_for: A learner might read what with as a question about what, when it introduces a reason.
A learner might take a plain with phrase to explain the main situation, when it can depict an accompanying circumstance.
teacher.activity: Students write sentences with with in two uses, one a depiction and one with what added as a reason, and say which is which.
